newsitem.title: USA: High Water on Ohio River closes some elevators.
newsitem.headline: High Water on Ohio River closes some elevators.

text.p: Rising water on the Ohio River which slowed barge traffic has forced the closure of several grain terminals in the Cincinnati area, river officials and industry sources said.

"There are several terminals that are closed in the Cincinnati area because the high water on the Ohio River made it impossible to load barges," said Jerry Knapper, marketing manager at Ingram Barge Co, based in Nashville, Tenn.
The problems began over the weekend when the Ohio River Basin was drenched by heavy rainfall.
"I expect that most of these terminals will not get back into business at least until the end of this week, depending on any additional rainfall," Knapper said.

Barge traffic between the Markland Dam near Lawrenceburg, Ind., and Meldal Dam, New Richmond, Ohio, was subject to length restrictions and can only navigate during daytime hours, U.S. Coast Guard Petty Officer Mike Sorlie, Marine Safety Detachment, Cincinnati, Sorlie said.
"There were no barges stranded near Cincinnati that we are aware of," Sorlie said. "But barge traffic has definitely slowed down."

One Cincinnati grain dealer who declined to be identified, said he was not sure when his facility on the Ohio River will open. "We are waiting for the crest tomorrow (Wednesday). We were not taking grain at all this week," he said.

At Cincinnati, the Ohio River early Tuesday had reached 62 feet, ten feet over flood stage at 52 feet, said Cathy Schuchter, public affairs specialist, Ohio River Division, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers at Cincinnati.
"The prediction for March 5 is that the river will rise to 63.7 feet. We expect the crest to be on March 5 at 64 feet around Wednesday evening," Schuchter said.
The worst flooding was in the Louisville, Ky., and Cincinnati areas and it fanned through West Virginia.
"The severe flooding started over the weekend as a storm swept across the Ohio River Basin resulting in flooding as far north as Parkersburg, West Virginia," she said.
Schuchter noted when the storm came through the Ohio River Valley Basin on Saturday and Sunday, some three to 13 inches of rain were dumped into the area.

Two waterway navigation projects were closed within the last 24 hours near Huntington, W. Va. Two additional waterway projects were expected to be closed, one in the Huntington area and the other, in the Cincinnati area, she said.
At Louisville, the flood stage for the Ohio River is 55 feet and Tuesday morning's reading was 66.5 feet.
"We expect that one to crest at 68.5 feet on March 7 in the afternoon," Schuchter said.
